title: Blood Transfusion Science and Immunohaematology
description: Blood group systems, grouping and antibody screening techniques, compatibility testing, donor selection and blood processing, and investigation of transfusion reactions and HDFN.

topics.title: ABO and Rh Blood Group Systems
topics.summary: ABO antigens and antibodies, inheritance, subgroups and the Bombay phenotype; the Rh system.

notes.b: The ABO system (Landsteiner, 1901) is the most important in transfusion. Antigens A and B are carbohydrate structures added to the H antigen by glycosyltransferases encoded by the ABO gene on chromosome 9; group O lacks these transferases and has the most H antigen. Naturally occurring antibodies (anti-A, anti-B — mainly IgM, reacting at room temperature, complement-fixing) are present in people lacking the corresponding antigen from about 3–6 months of age. Group O individuals also have anti-A,B (partly IgG, can cross the placenta). Subgroups (A1, A2) differ in antigen strength. The Bombay phenotype (Oh) lacks H antigen and has anti-H, so can only receive Oh blood. Approximate distribution in Nigeria: group O about half the population, followed by A and B, with AB least common.
k: A and B built on H antigen
Group O most common in Nigeria

notes.b: The Rh system is highly complex (D, C, c, E, e antigens); D is the most immunogenic. RhD-negative people lack D antigen and do not have anti-D naturally — anti-D is immune (IgG), formed after exposure through transfusion or pregnancy; it crosses the placenta and causes haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (HDFN) and haemolytic transfusion reactions. Rh-negative frequency is low in Nigeria (about 2–5%) compared with about 15% in white populations. Weak D and partial D variants complicate typing. Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis prevents sensitisation of RhD-negative mothers.

topics.title: Grouping, Antibody Screening and Compatibility Techniques
topics.summary: Forward and reverse grouping, the antiglobulin test, antibody screening and cross-matching.

notes.b: ABO grouping includes forward (cell) grouping — testing patient red cells with anti-A, anti-B (and anti-A,B) reagents — and reverse (serum/plasma) grouping — testing patient serum with known A1 and B cells. Both must agree; discrepancies (e.g. weak antigens, missing antibodies in neonates or the elderly, rouleaux, cold autoantibodies, recent transfusion) must be resolved before issuing blood. Reverse grouping is not done on neonates (antibodies are maternal or absent). RhD typing uses anti-D reagents (monoclonal); weak D testing may use the indirect antiglobulin technique. Methods: tile/slide (rapid, used in emergencies), tube, microplate and column agglutination (gel card) technology.

The antiglobulin (Coombs') test detects IgG or complement on red cells using anti-human globulin (AHG). The direct antiglobulin test (DAT) detects in vivo sensitisation (autoimmune haemolysis, HDFN, haemolytic transfusion reactions); the indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) detects antibodies in serum that coat red cells in vitro at 37 °C (antibody screening, cross-matching, weak D testing). Antibody screening tests patient serum against group O reagent cells of known antigen profile to detect clinically significant alloantibodies (anti-D, anti-K (Kell), anti-Fya (Duffy), anti-Jka (Kidd) — Kidd antibodies are notorious for delayed haemolytic reactions). The cross-match (compatibility test) tests patient serum against donor red cells by IAT (full cross-match) or electronically/immediate spin when the antibody screen is negative. False negatives in IAT arise from inadequate washing (neutralising AHG) — validated with IgG-coated control cells.

topics.title: Donor Selection, Blood Collection and Processing
topics.summary: Donor eligibility, collection, anticoagulants, component preparation and storage.

notes.b: Blood donors should be healthy voluntary non-remunerated donors aged about 18–65 years (national criteria vary), weighing at least 50 kg, with adequate haemoglobin (e.g. ≥ 12.5 g/dL), normal vital signs, and no high-risk behaviour or recent illness. Deferrals include recent malaria or fever, pregnancy and lactation, recent tattoo, certain drugs, and positive infection markers. About 450 mL (± 10%) is collected into bags containing anticoagulant–preservative: CPDA-1 (citrate — anticoagulant by chelating calcium; phosphate — buffer; dextrose — red cell energy; adenine — maintains ATP; shelf life 35 days at 2–6 °C). Additive solutions (SAGM) extend red cell storage to 42 days. Mandatory screening in Nigeria: HIV, hepatitis B (HBsAg), hepatitis C and syphilis; malaria testing is recommended in endemic areas.

Whole blood is centrifuged to prepare: packed red cells (2–6 °C), platelet concentrate (20–24 °C with continuous agitation; 5 days — highest risk of bacterial contamination), fresh frozen plasma (frozen within hours of collection, stored ≤ −25 °C for up to about 1–3 years depending on temperature; thawed at 37 °C), and cryoprecipitate (from slowly thawed FFP; rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII and vWF). Storage lesions of red cells include falling 2,3-DPG and ATP, rising potassium and haemolysis. Leucodepletion reduces febrile reactions, alloimmunisation and CMV transmission; irradiation prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in immunocompromised recipients. Blood bank refrigerators must have temperature monitoring and alarms.

topics.title: Transfusion Reactions and Haemovigilance
topics.summary: Laboratory investigation of reactions, TRALI, TACO, and haemovigilance systems.

notes.b: When a transfusion reaction is suspected: stop the transfusion, keep the IV line open with saline, check the patient's identity against the unit, return the bag and giving set to the laboratory, and send post-transfusion blood and urine samples. Laboratory investigation: clerical check; repeat ABO and RhD grouping on pre- and post-transfusion patient samples and the donor unit; direct antiglobulin test (positive in immune haemolysis); visual inspection of plasma for haemolysis; bilirubin, LDH and haptoglobin; urinalysis for haemoglobinuria; repeat antibody screen and cross-match; blood cultures of the patient and unit if bacterial contamination is suspected; coagulation screen for DIC. Acute haemolytic reactions are usually due to ABO incompatibility from identification errors.

Other reactions: febrile non-haemolytic (cytokines/leucocyte antibodies — reduced by leucodepletion), allergic/urticarial (plasma proteins; anaphylaxis in IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA), TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury — acute hypoxaemia and bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours, due to donor anti-HLA/HNA antibodies, typically from multiparous female donor plasma), TACO (transfusion-associated circulatory overload — hypertension, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema; treat with diuretics and slow transfusion), delayed haemolytic reaction (days later — falling Hb, jaundice, positive DAT), post-transfusion purpura, iron overload (chronic transfusion — chelation), and transfusion-transmitted infections. Haemovigilance is the systematic surveillance of adverse events across the transfusion chain to improve safety; Nigeria's National Blood Service Agency coordinates blood services and reporting.
k: TRALI: hypoxia within 6 h; donor antibodies
Delayed haemolytic: positive DAT days later

topics.title: Haemolytic Disease of the Fetus and Newborn
topics.summary: Mechanism, ABO and Rh HDFN, antenatal testing, anti-D prophylaxis and neonatal management.

notes.b: HDFN occurs when maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells carrying the corresponding antigen. RhD HDFN: an RhD-negative mother sensitised by a previous RhD-positive pregnancy (fetomaternal haemorrhage at delivery, miscarriage, abortion, ectopic pregnancy, trauma, amniocentesis) or transfusion produces anti-D; subsequent RhD-positive fetuses may develop severe anaemia, hydrops fetalis, jaundice and kernicterus. ABO HDFN is the most common form, occurring in first pregnancies because group O mothers have IgG anti-A,B; it is usually mild (jaundice), with a weakly positive DAT and spherocytes. Other antibodies causing HDFN include anti-c and anti-Kell (which suppresses fetal erythropoiesis).
k: ABO HDFN: commonest, mild, first pregnancy

notes.b: Antenatal testing: ABO and RhD grouping and antibody screening at booking and at 28 weeks for all pregnant women; titration or quantification of anti-D, and fetal monitoring by middle cerebral artery Doppler for anaemia; intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia. Prevention: anti-D immunoglobulin for non-sensitised RhD-negative women — routine antenatal prophylaxis (e.g. at 28–34 weeks) and within 72 hours after delivery of an RhD-positive baby or any sensitising event; the Kleihauer–Betke test (acid elution) quantifies fetomaternal haemorrhage to adjust the anti-D dose. Neonatal investigations: cord blood Hb, bilirubin, blood group and DAT. Treatment: phototherapy, exchange transfusion (with group O RhD-negative blood cross-matched against maternal plasma) and IVIG in selected cases.

Exchange transfusion with O RhD-negative blood
